script.opening: "I’ve had these scaly patches on my elbows, knees and scalp for years — they flare up, the creams barely touch them, and they’re back worse than ever. Honestly it’s wrecking my confidence; I cover up even in summer. And lately my fingers and lower back are stiff and achy in the mornings. Can you give me something stronger that actually works?"

facts.text: Psoriasis since age 20. Thick, red, scaly patches on both elbows and knees, scalp "flaky all the time", a patch in the small of the back. Worse over the last 6 months. Will show his elbows to the camera if asked: raised red plaques with silvery scale.

Has a steroid cream and a "vitamin D one" plus an emollient. Uses them "when it flares and stops when it calms down". Finds them greasy and messy, and two creams at different times "too much hassle". Uses an ordinary dandruff shampoo for the scalp.
If asked: "a few little dents" in his fingernails, and one nail lifting at the end.

For about 4 months: fingers stiff and achy in the mornings for about an hour; the end of his right middle finger "looked a bit puffy" a few weeks ago. Low back stiff first thing, better once he gets moving, wakes him in the early hours sometimes. No injury. No eye problems.
Stressful year — promoted to site manager. Drinks about 25 units a week, smokes 15 a day. BMI about 31. Not on beta-blockers or lithium; no new tablets. No recent sore throat.
No other conditions he knows of; blood pressure "never checked". No allergies. Father had a heart attack at 58 and also had psoriasis.

Dreads summer, never wears short sleeves, avoids swimming with his kids. Feels people stare. "It gets me down — not all the time, but it does." No thoughts of self-harm if asked. Partner, Joy, is supportive.

Frustrated, a little embarrassed. You want a stronger cream. Mention the joint stiffness in the opening but don’t expand unless asked. If the doctor explores the impact on your life, open up. Prefer one treatment at night if given the choice. Be surprised that the joints and heart risk might be linked.

ice.ideas: "The creams don’t work. I need something stronger — maybe tablets or an injection."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — the effect on his confidence and mood; covering up and avoiding the beach with his children. Also worried the stiff fingers mean he’s getting arthritis "like an old man", which would affect his job.
ice.expectations: "Something that actually clears it, so I can stop hiding."

cues: "I use them when it flares and stop when it calms down" — how he actually uses the creams.
"My fingers and lower back are stiff in the mornings" — possible psoriatic arthritis.
"I cover up even in summer" — the psychosocial impact to explore.

checkpoints.text: Recognises CHRONIC PLAQUE PSORIASIS (well-demarcated silvery-scaled plaques at extensor sites/scalp ± nail changes, chronic relapsing course) and assesses extent/severity/sites

Applies the topical TREATMENT LADDER — emollients + potent topical corticosteroid once daily and vitamin D analogue once daily applied separately (a combined product only if separate application is not possible) first-line for up to 4 weeks, site-appropriate preparations, review at 4 weeks and at least 4-week breaks between potent steroid courses (NICE CG153) — recognising "creams don’t work" is often under-treatment/incorrect application
Knows when to STEP UP/refer to dermatology (extensive/severe, topical-resistant, significant impact → phototherapy/systemics/biologics) and the urgent emergencies (erythrodermic/generalised pustular)

SCREENS for PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS (morning stiffness/joint pain, dactylitis, nail disease; PEST for peripheral joints, NICE NG65 criteria for the inflammatory back pain, joint exam face to face) and refers to RHEUMATOLOGY if suspected — not treating skin and missing joints

Recognises the CARDIOVASCULAR/metabolic comorbidity (assess/address smoking, weight, alcohol, BP/lipids/glucose; formal cardiovascular risk assessment for severe psoriasis at presentation and at least 5-yearly, CG153) and identifies TRIGGERS (stress, infection, skin trauma, drugs — beta-blockers/lithium/antimalarials)
Takes the PSYCHOSOCIAL impact seriously — confidence, mood, body image, stigma, relationships — screens low mood, and validates the distress rather than treating it as merely cosmetic
Explains the treatment plan and realistic expectations (control not cure), checks understanding (including correct application), and supports adherence

Safety-nets and follows up: optimised topical therapy with review, rheumatology referral for suspected psoriatic arthritis, cardiovascular/metabolic risk management, trigger advice, mood support, and dermatology referral if needed — treating more than the skin

worked.txt: "Those silvery, well-defined scaly patches on your elbows, knees and scalp are classic psoriasis — and importantly it’s more than a skin problem, so I want to look at the whole picture, not just hand you a stronger cream."

"Often ‘creams don’t work’ because the strength or how they’re used isn’t quite right. The mainstay is a strong steroid once a day and a vitamin D cream once a day, used separately — one in the morning, one at night — for up to 4 weeks, plus a proper scalp preparation, used consistently, with emollients underneath. Let’s get that right and review; if it’s still not controlled, the skin specialists have light therapy and tablets/injections."

"The morning stiffness in your fingers and back is important — psoriasis can come with a linked arthritis, and treating it early protects the joints. I’ll ask a few screening questions, including about your back, and examine your joints in person, and refer you to rheumatology if it fits."

"Psoriasis is also linked with heart and metabolic risk, so I’d like to check your blood pressure, cholesterol and sugar and support things like smoking, weight and alcohol. And some triggers matter — stress, infections, even certain blood-pressure tablets can flare it."

"You said it’s wrecking your confidence and you cover up — that matters as much as the skin itself. It’s really common for psoriasis to affect mood. How have you been in yourself? We can support that too, and good control usually helps the confidence."

"So: optimise the treatment and review, screen and refer for the joints, check your heart/metabolic risk, and look after your mood. Come back if it spreads dramatically, your skin goes red all over or you feel unwell — those rarer severe forms need urgent care. We’ll tackle this properly, not just paper over it."

f.learning: CHRONIC PLAQUE PSORIASIS — well-demarcated, red/salmon-pink plaques with SILVERY scale at extensor sites (elbows, knees), the scalp, and sometimes the lower back/umbilicus, often with NAIL changes (pitting, onycholysis) and a chronic relapsing course — must be managed as MORE THAN SKIN. Confirm the clinical picture and assess extent, severity and sites, then apply the topical TREATMENT LADDER: generous emollients plus a potent topical CORTICOSTEROID + VITAMIN D ANALOGUE (NICE CG153: once daily each, applied separately, for up to 4 weeks; a combined once-daily product only if separate application is not possible) first-line, with site-appropriate preparations (scalp formulations; appropriate agents for flexures/face) and review at 4 weeks, with at least 4-week breaks between courses of potent steroids at one site — recognising that "creams don’t work" is often under-treatment or incorrect potency/application. Know when to STEP UP or REFER to dermatology (extensive/severe, topical-resistant, significant functional/psychological impact, difficult sites → phototherapy, systemics such as methotrexate/ciclosporin/acitretin, biologics) and the rare emergencies (erythrodermic or generalised pustular psoriasis). Critically, SCREEN for PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS — morning joint stiffness/pain, dactylitis, enthesitis, axial symptoms or nail disease (PEST for peripheral joints, which misses axial disease; NICE NG65 inflammatory back pain criteria for the back; joints examined face to face) — and refer to rheumatology if suspected, because early treatment prevents joint damage; do not treat the skin and miss the joints. Recognise psoriasis as a SYSTEMIC condition associated with increased cardiovascular risk and metabolic syndrome (address smoking, weight, alcohol, BP/lipids/glucose, with formal cardiovascular risk assessment for severe psoriasis at presentation and at least every 5 years per CG153) and identify TRIGGERS (stress, infection — e.g. streptococcal/guttate, skin trauma/Koebner, and drugs such as beta-blockers, lithium, antimalarials, plus alcohol). Above all, take the PSYCHOSOCIAL impact seriously — psoriasis profoundly affects confidence, mood, body image, relationships and work, with stigma and real risk of depression/anxiety — so screen low mood and validate the distress rather than treating it as merely cosmetic. The hidden agenda is the visible skin plus the distress and now the joints; optimise treatment, screen arthritis and comorbidity, and address the emotional impact.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE CG153 Psoriasis: assessment and management (2012, updated 2017) · [2] NICE QS40 Psoriasis (2013) · [3] NICE NG65 Spondyloarthritis in over 16s (2017) · [4] MHRA Drug Safety Update December 2018 (emollients and fire risk) · [5] MHRA Drug Safety Update September 2021 (topical corticosteroid withdrawal reactions) · [6] BNF
knowledge.summary: Chronic plaque psoriasis with a big impact on confidence, now with inflammatory-sounding joint and back symptoms. Optimise topicals using the CG153 sequence, assess severity and impact, screen for psoriatic arthritis and refer to rheumatology, consider dermatology referral for major impact on wellbeing, and look at mood and cardiovascular risk.

points.t: CG153 [1] asks for a static Physician’s Global Assessment and body surface area, nail and difficult-site involvement, and the impact on physical, psychological and social wellbeing (DLQI in adults), plus assessment for depression. QS40 [2] sets severity and impact assessment as a quality statement.

points.h: Trunk and limbs: the topical sequence
points.t: CG153 [1]: start with a potent corticosteroid once daily plus a vitamin D preparation once daily, applied separately (one in the morning, one in the evening), for up to 4 weeks. If not controlled after a maximum of 8 weeks, switch to vitamin D twice daily; if still not controlled after 8–12 weeks, a potent corticosteroid twice daily for up to 4 weeks, or coal tar. A combined calcipotriol and betamethasone product once daily for up to 4 weeks is for people who cannot use separate applications. Review 4 weeks after starting a new topical in adults.

Scalp: a potent corticosteroid once daily for up to 4 weeks first, with a descaling agent or emollient beforehand if scale is thick [1]. Face, flexures and genitals: a mild or moderate corticosteroid for no longer than 2 weeks; do not use potent or very potent steroids there [1]. Aim for a break of at least 4 weeks between courses of potent or very potent steroids at one site.

CG153 [1] advises annual screening with the PEST questionnaire (it does not detect axial disease) and referral to a rheumatologist as soon as psoriatic arthritis is suspected. NG65 [3] refers adults with back pain that started before 45 and has lasted over 3 months if 4 or more features are present, and psoriasis is one of them. His finger stiffness and lower back symptoms need assessment now.

CG153 [1]: same-day referral for generalised pustular psoriasis or erythroderma. Refer when the diagnosis is uncertain, psoriasis is extensive (for example more than 10% of body surface area), it cannot be controlled with topical therapy, nail disease has a major impact, or any type has a major impact on physical, psychological or social wellbeing.

Assess and treat depression and anxiety. CG153 [1] offers a cardiovascular risk assessment to adults with severe psoriasis at presentation and at least every 5 years. Ask about smoking, alcohol and weight, and about drugs that can worsen psoriasis. Paraffin and other emollients soaked into fabric are a fire hazard [4].

model.text: Hello Daniel, it’s Dr Patel. Thanks for booking. Tell me what’s been going on with your skin.

These scaly patches on my elbows, knees and scalp. I’ve had them for years, they flare up, the creams barely touch them, and now they’re worse than ever. It’s wrecking my confidence, I cover up even in summer. And lately my fingers and lower back are stiff and achy in the mornings. Can you give me something stronger?

That sounds really frustrating, and the effect on your confidence matters to me as much as the skin. You’ve also mentioned the stiffness, which I want to come back to. Can we look at the skin, the joints, and how it’s affecting you, and then decide on a plan together?
model.why: Acknowledges impact and sets an agenda that includes the joints

model.text: Yes, fine.
Could you show me the elbows and knees on camera, in good light? And tell me which creams you’ve used and how you put them on.
These are the elbows. I’ve had a few creams. I use them when it flares and stop when it calms down. They’re greasy.

Thank you. The patches are well defined, red with silvery scale, which fits psoriasis. Is the scalp itchy or flaky under the hair? Any patches in the skin folds or groin? And have you noticed pitting or lifting of your nails?
Scalp’s bad, flaky all the time. Nails, maybe a few little dents.
Has anything set off this flare, such as stress, an illness, sore throat, or any new tablets?
model.why: Checks triggers including drugs and infection

model.text: Not that I know of. No new tablets.
Now the stiffness. How long does it last in the morning? Does it ease with moving or get worse? Any swollen fingers or toes, or pain at the heel?
model.why: Screens for inflammatory arthritis, dactylitis and enthesitis

model.text: A while. It gets better once I’m moving. Not sure about swelling.
And the back: when did that start, and does it wake you in the second half of the night or improve with exercise?
It’s been a while now. It does get better when I move about.

Morning stiffness that eases with movement, in someone with psoriasis and nail changes, can be psoriatic arthritis. It’s important because early treatment protects the joints. I’ll ask you to fill in a short questionnaire, and I’d like to examine your hands, feet and back in person this week.
model.why: Names PsA risk; PEST and face-to-face joint examination

model.text: I didn’t know the two were linked.
You said it’s wrecking your confidence. How is it affecting you day to day, and how has your mood been?
model.why: Explores psychosocial impact and screens mood

model.text: I dread summer. I don’t wear short sleeves. It gets me down, not all the time, but it does.
Thank you for being open. Has it ever got so low that you’ve had thoughts of harming yourself?
No, nothing like that.
What were you hoping a stronger cream would do?
Clear it, so I can stop hiding.

Creams often seem not to work because they’re used only in flares or not long enough, and that’s really common. There is no cure, but good control is realistic. I’d like to set you up with a clear routine: a strong steroid once a day and a vitamin D cream once a day, one in the morning and one at night, for four weeks, with a moisturiser as well. If the two separately don’t fit your day, there’s a combined gel once a day.
model.why: Explains CG153 sequence and addresses adherence

model.text: One thing at night would be easier for me.
Then we’ll use the combined one at night. For the scalp, a steroid scalp application once a day for four weeks, softening the scale first. I’ll review you in four weeks.

Because it’s having such a big effect on you, I’d also like to refer you to dermatology. They can offer light treatment, tablets or injections if the creams aren’t enough. And I’ll refer you to rheumatology about the joints once I’ve examined you.
model.why: Dermatology referral for major impact; rheumatology for suspected PsA

model.text: That would be good. I didn’t think I’d qualify.

Psoriasis is linked with heart and circulation risk too, so when you come in I’ll check your blood pressure and weight and arrange cholesterol and sugar tests. We can also talk about smoking and alcohol, which can make psoriasis worse.
Okay.

One safety point: moisturisers soaked into clothes or bedding can catch fire easily, so keep away from flames. If your skin becomes red all over, you get pus spots across it, or you feel unwell with it, that needs same-day care. And if your mood drops, please tell me. What will you do differently from tonight?
model.why: Emollient fire risk, emergency red flags, mood safety-net, teach-back

model.text: Combined gel every night for four weeks, not just when it’s bad, scalp stuff daily, moisturiser, and come in this week for the joints.
Spot on. I’ll send you the questionnaire and book the examination this week, then review in four weeks.

social.t: Covering up and avoiding summer are forms of social withdrawal. Ask about work, relationships and activities he avoids.
Greasy treatments are hard to use before work. Choosing times and products that fit his day improves adherence.

legal.t: Psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis with a substantial, long-term effect on daily activities may count as a disability, giving a right to reasonable adjustments at work.
If joint symptoms or a severe flare affect his work, a fit note can suggest adjustments such as altered duties.

professional.t: A camera view can show plaques but not joints. Arrange a face-to-face examination rather than referring or reassuring on the video alone.
State the site, potency, frequency and duration of each steroid, and plan a break between courses. Warn about emollient fire risk (MHRA December 2018).

community.t: The Psoriasis Association and the Psoriasis and Psoriatic Arthritis Alliance (PAPAA) offer information and peer support; talking therapies if mood is affected.

redFlags: Skin red all over (erythroderma) or widespread pustules: same day
Feeling unwell or feverish with a severe flare
Inflammatory joint symptoms, dactylitis or enthesitis
Low mood with thoughts of self-harm
psychosocial: Covering up, avoiding summer, effect on work and relationships
How and when he uses his creams
ice: Idea: the creams don’t work, so he needs something stronger
Concern: confidence, and new joint stiffness
Expectation: to clear it so he can stop hiding

playbook.diagnosis: “This is plaque psoriasis. The creams haven’t had a fair chance because they’ve been used only in flares. The stiffness may be a linked arthritis that we need to check properly.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “In psoriasis, the skin renews itself far faster than normal, so cells pile up as thick scaly patches. The immune system drives it, and the same process can inflame joints. Daily treatment keeps it calm, like a thermostat, rather than only firefighting.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted something stronger so you could stop hiding. Using the right treatment every day, plus a specialist opinion, gives you the best chance of that.”
management.psychosocial: Fit the routine to his day (combined product at night), refer to dermatology because of the impact on wellbeing, and support his mood.
sharedPlan: CG153 topical sequence: combined calcipotriol and betamethasone once daily at night for up to 4 weeks, as separate applications don’t suit him
Scalp: potent steroid scalp application once daily for up to 4 weeks, after softening scale
PEST, face-to-face joint examination, rheumatology referral if psoriatic arthritis suspected
Dermatology referral; BP, weight, lipids, HbA1c
safetyNet: Same-day care for widespread redness, pustules or feeling unwell

pitfalls.intro: This station is not about naming the strongest cream. It tests whether you find the adherence problem, catch the joints, and take the psychological impact seriously.

items.fail: Stepping up to a very potent steroid on request.
items.why: CG153 keeps very potent steroids for specialist settings on the trunk and limbs; the problem here is intermittent use.
items.fix: Ask how the creams were used, then give the CG153 routine with a 4-week review.

items.why: Psoriatic arthritis can damage joints if treatment is delayed; CG153 advises referral as soon as it is suspected.
items.fix: Ask about duration, relief with movement, dactylitis, enthesitis and back pain; examine face to face.

items.fail: Using PEST alone for the back pain.
items.why: PEST does not detect axial disease.
items.fix: Ask the NG65 inflammatory back pain questions too.

items.fail: Treating the confidence issue as cosmetic.
items.why: CG153 asks for assessment of impact and depression; major impact is itself a referral criterion.
items.fix: Ask about mood and daily impact, and let the answer shape the plan.

items.why: Topical plans need a 4-week review; erythroderma and pustular psoriasis need same-day care.
items.fix: Book the review and name the red flags.

items.why: The patient needs a routine he understands.
items.fix: “One gel every night for four weeks, then we check.”

avoid.dont: “Here’s a stronger steroid, use it when it flares.”
avoid.instead: “Let’s use the treatment every day for four weeks, then review, rather than only in flares.”
avoid.why: Intermittent use is the commonest reason creams seem to fail; a stronger steroid alone adds side-effects.

avoid.dont: “The stiffness is probably just your age.”
avoid.instead: “Stiffness that eases with movement can be arthritis linked to psoriasis, so I want to examine you.”
avoid.why: Missing psoriatic arthritis allows joint damage.

avoid.dont: “It’s only skin, lots of people have it.”

avoid.why: Minimising the impact loses Relating to Others marks and misses low mood.

Psoriasis is linked with heart and circulation risk too, so when you come in I’ll check your blood pressure and weight and arrange cholesterol and sugar tests. We can also talk about smoking and alcohol, which can make psoriasis worse.
Okay.

One safety point: moisturisers soaked into clothes or bedding can catch fire easily, so keep away from flames. If your skin becomes red all over, you get pus spots across it, or you feel unwell with it, that needs same-day care. And if your mood drops, please tell me. What will you do differently from tonight?

SCA_MODELS.text: Combined gel every night for four weeks, not just when it’s bad, scalp stuff daily, moisturiser, and come in this week for the joints.
Spot on. I’ll send you the questionnaire and book the examination this week, then review in four weeks.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE CG153 Psoriasis: assessment and management (2012, updated 2017) · [2] NICE QS40 Psoriasis (2013) · [3] NICE NG65 Spondyloarthritis in over 16s (2017) · [4] MHRA Drug Safety Update December 2018 (emollients and fire risk) · [5] MHRA Drug Safety Update September 2021 (topical corticosteroid withdrawal reactions) · [6] BNF
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Chronic plaque psoriasis with a big impact on confidence, now with inflammatory-sounding joint and back symptoms. Optimise topicals using the CG153 sequence, assess severity and impact, screen for psoriatic arthritis and refer to rheumatology, consider dermatology referral for major impact on wellbeing, and look at mood and cardiovascular risk.

points.t: CG153 [1] asks for a static Physician’s Global Assessment and body surface area, nail and difficult-site involvement, and the impact on physical, psychological and social wellbeing (DLQI in adults), plus assessment for depression. QS40 [2] sets severity and impact assessment as a quality statement.

points.h: Trunk and limbs: the topical sequence
points.t: CG153 [1]: start with a potent corticosteroid once daily plus a vitamin D preparation once daily, applied separately (one in the morning, one in the evening), for up to 4 weeks. If not controlled after a maximum of 8 weeks, switch to vitamin D twice daily; if still not controlled after 8–12 weeks, a potent corticosteroid twice daily for up to 4 weeks, or coal tar. A combined calcipotriol and betamethasone product once daily for up to 4 weeks is for people who cannot use separate applications. Review 4 weeks after starting a new topical in adults.

Scalp: a potent corticosteroid once daily for up to 4 weeks first, with a descaling agent or emollient beforehand if scale is thick [1]. Face, flexures and genitals: a mild or moderate corticosteroid for no longer than 2 weeks; do not use potent or very potent steroids there [1]. Aim for a break of at least 4 weeks between courses of potent or very potent steroids at one site.

CG153 [1] advises annual screening with the PEST questionnaire (it does not detect axial disease) and referral to a rheumatologist as soon as psoriatic arthritis is suspected. NG65 [3] refers adults with back pain that started before 45 and has lasted over 3 months if 4 or more features are present, and psoriasis is one of them. His finger stiffness and lower back symptoms need assessment now.

CG153 [1]: same-day referral for generalised pustular psoriasis or erythroderma. Refer when the diagnosis is uncertain, psoriasis is extensive (for example more than 10% of body surface area), it cannot be controlled with topical therapy, nail disease has a major impact, or any type has a major impact on physical, psychological or social wellbeing.

Assess and treat depression and anxiety. CG153 [1] offers a cardiovascular risk assessment to adults with severe psoriasis at presentation and at least every 5 years. Ask about smoking, alcohol and weight, and about drugs that can worsen psoriasis. Paraffin and other emollients soaked into fabric are a fire hazard [4].

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Let him describe the skin, the impact and the joints before narrowing; acknowledged frustration.
Work and routine, covering up, summer avoidance, smoking and alcohol flagged for review.
Picked up the morning stiffness and “wrecking my confidence” and explored both.
Idea (creams don’t work, needs stronger), concern (confidence, joints), expectation (to clear it and stop hiding).
Camera look at plaques, scalp and nails; PEST; face-to-face joint and back examination; BP, weight, lipids, HbA1c.
Plaque psoriasis with suboptimal topical use; psoriatic arthritis; axial spondyloarthritis; triggers.
Screened for erythroderma and pustular psoriasis, and for low mood and self-harm.
Named chronic plaque psoriasis, likely under-treated, with possible psoriatic arthritis.
CG153 topical sequence with a combined product for adherence, scalp treatment, dermatology referral for major impact.
Rheumatology referral if PsA confirmed on examination; cardiovascular risk and mood addressed.
Review at 4 weeks, same-day triggers, emollient fire safety, mood safety-net.

social.t: Covering up and avoiding summer are forms of social withdrawal. Ask about work, relationships and activities he avoids.
Greasy treatments are hard to use before work. Choosing times and products that fit his day improves adherence.

legal.t: Psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis with a substantial, long-term effect on daily activities may count as a disability, giving a right to reasonable adjustments at work.
If joint symptoms or a severe flare affect his work, a fit note can suggest adjustments such as altered duties.

professional.t: A camera view can show plaques but not joints. Arrange a face-to-face examination rather than referring or reassuring on the video alone.
State the site, potency, frequency and duration of each steroid, and plan a break between courses. Warn about emollient fire risk (MHRA December 2018).

community.t: The Psoriasis Association and the Psoriasis and Psoriatic Arthritis Alliance (PAPAA) offer information and peer support; talking therapies if mood is affected.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is plaque psoriasis. The creams haven’t had a fair chance because they’ve been used only in flares. The stiffness may be a linked arthritis that we need to check properly.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “In psoriasis, the skin renews itself far faster than normal, so cells pile up as thick scaly patches. The immune system drives it, and the same process can inflame joints. Daily treatment keeps it calm, like a thermostat, rather than only firefighting.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted something stronger so you could stop hiding. Using the right treatment every day, plus a specialist opinion, gives you the best chance of that.”
management.psychosocial: Fit the routine to his day (combined product at night), refer to dermatology because of the impact on wellbeing, and support his mood.
sharedPlan: CG153 topical sequence: combined calcipotriol and betamethasone once daily at night for up to 4 weeks, as separate applications don’t suit him
Scalp: potent steroid scalp application once daily for up to 4 weeks, after softening scale
PEST, face-to-face joint examination, rheumatology referral if psoriatic arthritis suspected
Dermatology referral; BP, weight, lipids, HbA1c
safetyNet: Same-day care for widespread redness, pustules or feeling unwell

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is not about naming the strongest cream. It tests whether you find the adherence problem, catch the joints, and take the psychological impact seriously.

items.fail: Stepping up to a very potent steroid on request.
items.why: CG153 keeps very potent steroids for specialist settings on the trunk and limbs; the problem here is intermittent use.
items.fix: Ask how the creams were used, then give the CG153 routine with a 4-week review.

items.why: Psoriatic arthritis can damage joints if treatment is delayed; CG153 advises referral as soon as it is suspected.
items.fix: Ask about duration, relief with movement, dactylitis, enthesitis and back pain; examine face to face.

items.fail: Using PEST alone for the back pain.
items.why: PEST does not detect axial disease.
items.fix: Ask the NG65 inflammatory back pain questions too.

items.fail: Treating the confidence issue as cosmetic.
items.why: CG153 asks for assessment of impact and depression; major impact is itself a referral criterion.
items.fix: Ask about mood and daily impact, and let the answer shape the plan.

items.why: Topical plans need a 4-week review; erythroderma and pustular psoriasis need same-day care.
items.fix: Book the review and name the red flags.

items.why: The patient needs a routine he understands.
items.fix: “One gel every night for four weeks, then we check.”
